extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, legal advocates, DHS rulemaking stakeholders, and members of the public commenting on the proposed DHS public-charge rule
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for which public benefits DHS proposes to consider (monetizable vs non-monetizable), and explicit exclusions/exceptions (e.g., emergency Medicaid, IDEA services, certain foreign-born children). Targets determinations of whether an alien is likely to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: SNAP considered as public-charge factor (monetizable)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to consider SNAP benefits because the program is among the largest Federal expenditures for low-income people, and because receipt of SNAP benefits indicates a lack of self-sufficiency in satisfying a basic living need, i.e., food and nutrition. SNAP, which is a non-cash, monetizable public benefit, provides nutrition assistance to low-income individuals and households who must meet certain income and resource limitations to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SNAP benefits are received on an EBT card and can be monetized; Disaster SNAP is excluded (provided under separate authority). The proposal treats SNAP like other monetizable non-cash benefits when assessing public-charge risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include high-expenditure housing benefits (Section 8, public housing)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to include certain high-expenditure housing-related benefits (Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers, Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance, and Public Housing) in public charge determinations because these programs impose significant expense on multiple levels of government and relate to a basic living need (shelter), so receipt suggests lack of self-sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS recognizes these programs have lower participation by noncitizens and different levels of expenditure than some other programs, but still proposes inclusion because total Federal expenditure remains significant. The proposal treats these housing programs as part of public-charge assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: HUD-subsidized and privately administered housing programs' income/eligibility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal and HUD programs provide low-income individuals and families with housing at below-market rent or rent subsidies; while programs vary, they commonly use the same or similar standards when establishing income eligibility and contribution toward rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 214 of the HCD Act of 1980 restricts HUD financial assistance to aliens unless they fit enumerated resident categories. The discussion notes programmatic variations but emphasizes shared income-eligibility approaches relevant to assessing benefit receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program characterized as monetizable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program is a non-cash public benefit that can be monetized; it provides assistance to very low-income families to afford decent, safe, and sanitary housing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants find suitable housing where owner agrees to rent; PHAs enter HAP contracts with landlords and pay subsidies based on HUD-established payment standards; participants pay the difference between actual rent and the subsidy. Under certain circumstances vouchers may be used to purchase homes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance characterized as monetizable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Section 8 Project-Based Rental Assistance Program (including Moderate Rehabilitation) is a non-cash but monetizable public benefit providing rental assistance for extremely low- to low-income households in private accommodations; HUD subsidies to private owners lower rental costs and offset construction/rehab costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rental assistance equals the difference between household ability-to-pay and approved rent for the unit. Contracts (HAP) are renewed for already-assisted units; authority for project-based assistance for new construction/substantial rehab was repealed in 1983.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicaid categorized as non-monetizable for 15% FPG standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Medicaid is a non-cash, non-monetizable public benefit — a joint Federal/state health coverage program available to needy persons meeting income/resource rules. DHS does not propose a methodology to monetize Medicaid benefits for purposes of the 15 percent of FPG standard and therefore would categorize Medicaid as a non-monetizable benefit under the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medicaid enrollment and receipt vary state-by-state and enrollee-to-enrollee; goods and services differ among recipients, making individual monetization difficult. DHS nonetheless recognizes Medicaid's large aggregate Federal expenditure and that participation generally indicates lack of self-sufficiency in satisfying medical care needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception: Emergency medical condition Medicaid services excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to except consideration of assistance for an 'emergency medical condition' as provided under 42 U.S.C. 1396b(v) and 42 CFR 440.255(c) from public-charge consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Emergency medical condition’ defined in 42 CFR 440.255(c) (acute symptoms of sufficient severity that immediate attention is needed to avoid serious jeopardy). States determine whether treatment falls under emergency condition and reimburse providers. Congress (PRWORA) specifically excluded emergency medical conditions from Federal public-benefit definitions; EM services are often involuntary and must be provided regardless of ability to pay. Case law shows state-by-state variation (examples: leukemia crises accepted as emergency in Szewczyk; prolonged chemo not necessarily emergency in Diaz). DHS will not consider such emergency treatment funded by Medicaid in public-charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception: IDEA and school-based services excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to exclude services or benefits under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) and school-based benefits provided to children at or below the oldest age eligible for secondary education from consideration in public-charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IDEA requires schools to provide special education and related services; states/school districts may bill Medicaid for costs where parents consent to release personally identifiable information. Reimbursements generally go to schools/LEAs, not individual parents/students, and are not income-based. Excluding these services helps ensure schools continue to receive funds and parents do not withhold consent for Medicaid billing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception: Medicaid receipt by foreign-born children of U.S. citizens excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to exclude consideration of receipt of all Medicaid benefits by foreign-born children (as defined in section 101(c)) who either have U.S. citizen parents, have been adopted by U.S. citizens, or are coming to be adopted by U.S. citizens, where such children will automatically acquire U.S. citizenship under section 320 or be eligible to naturalize under section 322.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion enumerates immigrant visa categories (IR-2/IR-7, IR-3/IR-8, IH-3, IR-4/IR-9, IH-4) and procedural notes (Forms I-130, I-600, I-800, N-600/N-600K). Cites Child Citizenship Act and Intercountry Adoption Act as protective frameworks designed to avoid adverse immigration consequences to foreign-born children of U.S. citizens; DHS would not consider these children's Medicaid receipt in public-charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of benefit receipt and Federal expenditure as indicators of self-sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS frames consideration of benefits by (1) whether the benefit relates to a basic living need (food, shelter, medical care) and thus indicates lack of self-sufficiency, and (2) the magnitude of Federal expenditure on the program as relevant to inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs that are non-cash but monetizable and serve basic needs may be treated as evidence of lack of self-sufficiency. DHS weighs programmatic characteristics (eligibility rules, monetizability, expenditure levels, noncitizen participation rates) and may nonetheless include programs even if noncitizen participation is currently low when overall Federal expenditures are significant. For programs difficult to monetize at the individual level (e.g., Medicaid), DHS may categorize them as non-monetizable and treat them differently (see Medicaid entry).
